Identifying Arhopala
from photographs

A personal tool — sharing it in case it helps others

Been building this for a while — an interactive version of the Corbet & Pendlebury dichotomous key for Malaysian Oakblue butterflies, rebuilt for field photographs where the upperside and forewing base aren't always visible. If you photograph Arhopala in Peninsular Malaysia, this might save you some time.

C&P+

Work through the key one couplet at a time

C&P+ is the main identification tool. Each screen shows a single couplet from the Corbet & Pendlebury key — one character statement, two choices. As you answer, the candidate list updates in real time: species consistent with your answers rise, the rest drop away.

The key starts with the first question — hindwing tailed? — and walks through morphological characters from there. 110 species at the start, narrowing with every step.

Key 0 — the starting question. 110 species in play.

Live ranking

Candidates ranked in real time as you answer

After a few answers the candidate panel fills with species, ordered by their consistency with your answers so far. Each row shows the species name and a score bar.

The breadcrumb trail beneath the topbar shows every couplet answered so far — tap any step to go back to it.

After 4 answers: 69 species still in play, the list visible below the current couplet card.

4 keys answered · 69 species left · candidates visible below the current couplet

Cannot determine — two paths

When FW spaces 2–3 aren't visible — fork option

Some couplets ask about forewing spaces 2–3 — the base of the wing that's usually hidden under the hindwing in resting shots. At these couplets a Cannot determine row appears below Yes/No.

At Key 155, both branches lead to further couplets, so "Cannot determine" opens two labelled paths: → Key 156 (spots not wider below vein 4) or → Key 192 (spots wider below vein 4). Follow whichever description matches — or try both.

No penalty: pressing either fork button does not eliminate any candidates — it just picks which branch to follow next.

Key 155 — "Cannot determine" expands into two labelled branch buttons

Cannot determine — single skip

When one branch terminates — single skip

At Key 161, branch B terminates at a single species (A. epimete) while branch A continues into further couplets. Pressing "Cannot determine" here routes silently to branch A — you continue through the key without committing to either Yes or No.

The breadcrumb records the step as "Skip → B" so you can always come back to it if you later get a better view of the forewing.

Key 161 — single "Cannot determine" that routes to branch A. 4 species left.

Back navigation

Step back anytime using the breadcrumb trail

Every answered couplet leaves a chip in the breadcrumb trail — tap any earlier key number to jump back to that step. Steps after the one you tapped are cleared, but everything before is preserved.

Skipped couplets show their skip direction: Key 24: Skip → B here. That label is a live reminder that this branch was skipped, and you can re-visit it if you find a photo where the character is visible.

No dead ends: tapping back and choosing the other branch is always available — useful when a character was hard to call.

"Key 24: Skip → B" in the trail — skipped couplet recorded, current is Key 46

Species Search

Validate your ID using Species Search

Once C&P+ points you toward a species, use Species Search to look it up directly. Search by name — results list matching taxa with their common names.

Each species page shows the diagnostic characters from the key, the numbered C&P key route, and the underside-only path summary (the couplets reachable from a typical resting photograph). Plus a link to iNaturalist observations for reference photos.

Sanity check: does the description on the species page match what you see in your photograph? If the characters don't line up, the key is pointing elsewhere.

Search returns matching species

Species detail — diagnostic characters, key path, iNat link

Give it a try

The key covers Arhopala recorded from Peninsular Malaysia — around 110 taxa, many cryptic. It works best from underside photographs and is designed to handle the common case where the upperside and forewing base aren't visible. If something seems wrong or a species is missing, the source is open and issues are welcome.
